claim: Parameter-based knowledge editing cannot reliably update factual knowledge in a large language model without damaging its core capabilities. The near-perfect editing results reported in prior work do not survive realistic evaluation, and the limitation is geometric rather than incidental: localized weight edits are disproportionately amplified along low-variance directions of the model's representation space and propagate globally, so damage compounds as edits accumulate. A parameter-free approach that leaves the weights untouched is therefore a serious alternative to parameter editing rather than a fallback.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaim 1, run a realistic head-to-head evaluation of parameter-based editors versus a parameter-free baseline. Use public datasets COUNTERFACT/COUNTERFACT+, ZSRE, RippleEdits, MQuAKE, Natural Questions, plus general-capability benchmarks such as MMLU, HellaSwag, LAMBADA, and GSM8K. On an open model such as GPT-J-6B or Llama-2-7B, compare ROME, MEMIT, MEND, constrained fine-tuning, and a parameter-free in-context or retrieval-based editing method such as IKE/RAG-style prompting. Evaluate not only single-prompt edit success, but paraphrase generalization, dynamic neighborhood locality, portability, multi-hop consistency, perplexity, and downstream task degradation before and after editing. Also verify the parameter-free method by hashing or checksuming model weights before and after use. If parameter editors retain high efficacy while preserving locality, perplexity, and general benchmark scores under this broader protocol, the claim that they cannot reliably update knowledge without damage is weakened. If their near-perfect edit scores collapse under paraphrases, dynamic neighborhoods, multi-hop tests, or general-capability checks while the parameter-free method is competitive, the claim is supported. This experiment could be made partly unnecessary by a large, independently replicated benchmark already reporting these exact metrics, confidence intervals, and unchanged-weight verification for parameter-free methods.

To address subclaim 6, perform a sequential and batch edit scaling study to test whether damage compounds as edits accumulate. Starting from the same base model and using recallable facts from COUNTERFACT, ZSRE, and MQuAKE-CF, apply edit counts k = 1, 10, 100, 1000, and, if feasible, 3000 with ROME, MEMIT, MEND, and constrained fine-tuning; include the best-performing parameter-free method from Experiment 1 as a non-weight-changing comparator. After each edit block, remeasure edit efficacy, paraphrase success, locality on unrelated and semantically adjacent facts, RippleEdits consistency, MQuAKE multi-hop accuracy, held-out Natural Questions accuracy, LAMBADA/WikiText perplexity, and MMLU/HellaSwag scores. Track whether earlier edits are forgotten and whether unrelated predictions drift. If degradation grows approximately monotonically or superlinearly with edit count, especially while individual edit success remains high, this supports the claim that damage compounds globally. If many edits can be accumulated with stable locality and stable general capability, the compounding-damage subclaim is weakened. This experiment could be avoided only if prior work already provided open logs for large-k sequential and batch editing with the same broad capability and locality measurements, not just edit-success scores.

To address subclaim 4, test the proposed geometric mechanism directly by measuring whether localized weight edits are amplified along low-variance representation directions. For the layers targeted by ROME/MEMIT or other editors, estimate the hidden-state covariance spectrum using public text such as WikiText-103, Wikipedia, or The Pile subsets available on HuggingFace. For each factual edit from COUNTERFACT or ZSRE, decompose the induced activation change and weight-update effect into the covariance eigenbasis, then measure amplification as a function of eigenvalue size and correlate it with downstream logit shifts on unrelated prompts, locality failures, and benchmark degradation. Include controls such as random low-norm updates matched in Frobenius norm, edits constrained away from low-variance directions, and edits projected onto high-variance directions. If harmful global logit shifts and locality failures are concentrated in low-variance eigendirections, and suppressing those components reduces damage while preserving edit success, the geometric subclaim is supported. If amplification is not related to representation variance, or if low-variance projections do not predict damage, the limitation looks less geometric and more method-specific or incidental. This experiment could be made unnecessary by released mechanistic analyses that already publish layerwise covariance spectra, edit decompositions, and causal tests linking low-variance directions to post-edit failures.
reference_experiments: Fix the measurement floor and the inference protocol before editing anything. Score the unedited model on the editing benchmark to establish the pre-edit baseline, and re-run single-edit evaluation of existing methods under plain autoregressive decoding rather than the teacher-forced protocol prior work used, since teacher forcing supplies the ground-truth answer tokens at inference and inflates every number. If methods keep their near-perfect single-edit scores under honest decoding there is no discrepancy to explain. The authors report a pre-edit baseline of Reliability 3.00, Generalization 3.00, Locality 15.50, Portability 4.36 on ZsRE, and a best parameter-based single-edit average of 25.99.

Validate the scoring instrument before quoting any number from it. Judge semantic consistency of generated answers with a strong LLM across reliability, generalization, locality and portability, then cross-check that ranking with a deterministic token-level measure (match ratio and exact match) that does not depend on a model's opinion. If the two disagree, every result is an artifact of the judge rather than a property of the editing methods. The authors find the token-level check reproduces the semantic ranking, with the pre-edit model at 100% by definition and GRACE holding 100% under both single and sequential editing.

Test the asserted mechanism directly. Take the SVD of the original hidden-representation matrix, compute the directional relative change rate R_k = sqrt(n)|u_k^T delta_h| / sigma_k for each principal direction after an edit, and check where amplification concentrates and how it behaves as edits accumulate. The claim's causal story requires R_k > 1 predominantly in low-singular-value directions with the fraction rising monotonically with edit count, across methods and architectures.

Run the main benchmark. Compare eleven editing methods spanning locate-then-edit (ROME, MEMIT, PMET, RECT, AlphaEdit, FT-L), meta-learning (MEND), additional-parameter (AdaLoRA, WISE) and external-memory (GRACE, SCR) families, under sequential editing at 1, 10, 100 and full-dataset edit counts, on ZsRE and WikiData-counterfact, across Llama-2-7B-Chat, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, reporting all four dimensions. The claim holds if every parameter-modifying method degrades toward zero as edits accumulate and the parameter-free retrieval baseline outscores all of them; the authors report ROME, RECT, FT-L, MEND and AdaLoRA at 0.00-0.25 average under sequential editing on DeepSeek-R1-Distill, against SCR at 56.59 single and 60.19 sequential.

Measure damage to capabilities the edits never targeted. Take the models edited in the main benchmark and evaluate them on mathematical reasoning (AIME 2024, AIME 2025, AMC, OlympiadBench, MATH-500) and broad benchmarks (GPQA-Diamond, ARC-c, MMLU-Pro), reporting accuracy after 10 and after 100 sequential edits. Without this the study would only show editing is ineffective, not that it is damaging. The authors report ROME and RECT losing 2.74 and 8.37 average accuracy at 10 edits and falling to near zero at 100, with MEND at 0.00 after both.

Rule out that the result is an artifact of scale, knowledge type, fact difficulty or one method's configuration. Repeat the sweep on larger models (Llama-2-13B, Qwen3-14B), on event-level knowledge (ELKEN, with events converted to triples for the parameter-based arms), split by high- and low-confidence fact sets, and probe the hyperparameter and architecture sensitivity of AlphaEdit — the one method that does not collapse — including its failure to run on Llama-2 and Mistral. If the collapse disappears at 13-14B or only occurs on triple-shaped facts, the claim is bounded rather than general.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A clean pre-edit baseline together with free-running autoregressive evaluation that reveals whether apparent single-edit gains depend on answer leakage during inference.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 explicitly calls for a realistic head-to-head evaluation of single-prompt edit success, evaluation before and after editing, and checks that would expose inflated or non-robust success under realistic prompting. A competent implementation of that protocol would use ordinary autoregressive generation rather than teacher forcing and retain an unedited comparison.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Independent validation of the semantic scoring instrument using a deterministic token-level measure, so method rankings are not attributable to the evaluator's subjective judgments.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed experiments list efficacy, generalization, locality, portability, perplexity, and downstream accuracy, but do not require an independent deterministic token-level check against the semantic evaluator or any decision rule for resolving disagreement between them.
reasoning_chain: [1] Reference experiment 1 establishes whether the reported semantic rankings survive an evaluator-independent token-level check.
[2] Proposed experiments measure editing and capability outcomes but never cross-check a semantic judge with a deterministic match or exact-match instrument.
[3] Without that cross-check, a team could observe a ranking while remaining unable to tell whether it reflects editing behavior or scoring-judge artifacts.
[4] The team would fail to learn what reference experiment 1 would have told them: whether the semantic evaluation itself is validated.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A direct, normalized directional analysis of representation changes that tests concentration in low-variance directions and its increase with edit count across methods and model settings.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 2 directly measures activation and weight-update components in a covariance eigenbasis and adds matched-norm and projection interventions, which is at least as discriminating for the low-variance-direction mechanism on the tested setup. Proposed experiment 1 supplies edit-count scaling, but only measures behavioral drift and damage, not the directional amplification statistic at each edit count. The combined set therefore does not establish that the low-variance amplification fraction itself rises monotonically with accumulated edits, nor does it provide a systematic cross-architecture test of that trajectory.
reasoning_chain: [1] Reference experiment 2 distinguishes the geometric mechanism from generic degradation by measuring normalized directional amplification and testing its concentration in low-variance directions as edits accumulate.
[2] Proposed experiment 2 can test the direction-variance association and causal effect of suppressing or emphasizing those directions.
[3] Proposed experiment 1 varies the number of edits but records behavioral efficacy, locality, and capability scores rather than directional amplification at those same counts.
[4] Behavioral degradation alone does not identify low-variance amplification or show that its fraction increases with edit count.

[5] A team running the proposed set could learn that low-variance components predict damage in an individual-edit setting, but would fail to learn whether the claimed directional amplification trajectory is the accumulating, cross-setting mechanism described by the reference experiment.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A realistic comparative benchmark covering representative parameter-modifying editing families and a weight-preserving alternative over increasing sequential edit loads, with factual success, generalization, locality, portability, and capability outcomes.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 supplies the head-to-head comparison, multiple factual and capability evaluations, and a parameter-free comparator. Proposed experiment 1 adds sequential and batch scaling through 1, 10, 100, 1000, and possibly 3000 edits while tracking efficacy, generalization, locality, multi-hop consistency, perplexity, and general capability. The proposal need not reproduce the reference's exact method count, datasets, or model list because the claim does not bind those incidental choices.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Post-edit measurement of unrelated, held-out reasoning and general capabilities at both modest and substantial sequential edit loads, with a clean comparison that separates capability damage from failure to edit the target facts.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 measures downstream task degradation before and after editing on broad capability and reasoning benchmarks. Proposed experiment 1 measures MMLU, HellaSwag, and related held-out capability outcomes after each sequential edit block, including the 10- and 100-edit regimes. These are different capability instruments from the reference but provide the same discriminating evidence about collateral damage.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Robustness evidence showing that the conclusion is not confined to one model scale, one knowledge representation or fact-difficulty regime, or one editor's hyperparameters and architecture configuration.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed set varies factual datasets, including single-hop and multi-hop settings, and compares several parameter-editing procedures, so it can expose some method- and data-specific failures. However, both proposed benchmark experiments are described on one selected base model, with no larger-model replication, event-level knowledge condition, explicit high- versus low-confidence split, or systematic hyperparameter and architecture-sensitivity sweep. The geometric controls in experiment 2 do not fill those omitted scope axes.
reasoning_chain: [1] Reference experiment 5 tests whether the claimed limitation persists across model scale, knowledge type, fact difficulty, and editor configuration rather than arising from one setup.
[2] Proposed experiments 0 and 1 vary datasets and several editing methods, providing partial cross-method and cross-content evidence.
[3] They do not vary model scale or architecture in a planned way, split facts by confidence or difficulty, test event-level knowledge separately, or sweep sensitive configurations.
[4] Repeating the behavioral study across several datasets and methods on one model can still be explained by a model-scale, knowledge-type, difficulty, or configuration confound.
[5] The team would fail to learn whether the conclusion generalizes across those omitted scales, knowledge forms, fact strata, and configurations.

runs.sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set directly addresses the main empirical comparison, sequential accumulation of damage, preservation of unrelated capabilities, the low-variance geometric mechanism, and verification that the parameter-free comparator leaves weights unchanged. It would therefore provide a substantial test of the claim. It would not fully settle the claim as broadly stated because the evaluation instrument is not independently validated, the directional mechanism is not explicitly tracked across edit counts and architectures, and robustness across scale, knowledge type, fact difficulty, and configuration is incomplete.
missing: An evaluator-independent deterministic token-level cross-check of the semantic editing scores, with a stated rule for handling disagreement.
Directional amplification measurements repeated at the same sequential edit counts and across multiple architectures or model settings.
Replications across model scale and architecture, event-level versus triple-shaped knowledge, fact-confidence/difficulty strata, and systematic hyperparameter/configuration sweeps.
